title: Respond to an acquisition approach
summary: Most corporate-development interest is market research; a real offer carries urgency and an expiration (lore rule kan-real-offer-test). Qualify the approach before the company feels it, and decide whether you have a concrete reason to sell at all (lore rule gil-legitimate-reasons-to-sell). If the conversation continues, the NDA comes before any data or team access (lore rule kan-nda-before-term-sheet), and the board hears about it before any exclusivity: a no-shop binds the company, and once the term sheet is signed you cannot shop the deal and unsettled points default to the acquirer (lore rule kan-leverage-ends-at-term-sheet). Decide who runs the process: M&A counsel always, a banker when the stage and the multiple justify the fee (lore rule dixon-banker-only-late-stage). Stand up a clean data room, research how this acquirer has behaved between LOI and close (lore rule dixon-research-loi-conduct), and prepare the leak playbook before there is anything to leak. Editorial guidance from the startup lore and the standard documents; nothing here is legal or financial advice.

parts.title: Qualify the approach: a real offer carries urgency and an expiration; corp-dev coffee without a clock is market research
parts.guidance: Treat the approach as real only when it carries an expiration date or a term sheet promised within days, with the acquirer applying the time pressure (lore rule kan-real-offer-test). Acquisitions happen when an internal champion wants to own you (lore rule kan-companies-are-bought-not-sold), so identify who the champion is before investing the company's attention. Engage at all only with a concrete reason to sell (lore rule gil-legitimate-reasons-to-sell).

execution.rationale: The founder reads the approach and the counterparty directly; qualifying intent is a judgment conversation.

parts.title: Sign the NDA before anything moves: no data, no architecture walkthroughs, no team interviews until it is signed
parts.guidance: Once committed to exploring a sale, share data freely under an NDA so red flags surface before the term sheet, and refuse acquirer interviews of your team until it is signed (lore rule kan-nda-before-term-sheet). The NDA is the gate between a conversation and a diligence process. If qualification said no, the response is a polite decline and the process ends; everything from here runs only on a real offer the founder chose to explore.
parts.when: the approach is real and the founder chooses to explore a sale

execution.rationale: Counsel adapts the NDA and the founder signs it; the refusal to share before signature is a human boundary to hold in live conversations.

parts.title: Tell the board before any exclusivity: a no-shop binds the company, and agreeing to one is a board-level decision

execution.rationale: The founder briefs the board directly; exclusivity trades away the company's alternatives and the directors own that call with the founder.

parts.title: Decide who runs the deal: M&A counsel always; a banker when the stage and the multiple justify the fee
parts.guidance: Use a banker only when the company is late stage and selling on a multiple of profits or revenue; earlier than that, the founder runs the process with counsel (lore rule dixon-banker-only-late-stage).

execution.rationale: The founder selects and engages counsel, and weighs a banker, through direct conversations; the engagement terms are negotiated personally.

parts.title: Stand up the deal data room with clean permissions, so diligence answers come from one controlled place

execution.rationale: The owner assembles and permissions the diligence materials in the chosen room; the referenced record carries the setup mechanics.

parts.title: Negotiate the big points before the term sheet: price, structure, and the non-price deal-killers
parts.guidance: Negotiate the business and legal points before signing and push for the shortest closing you can get; after signing you cannot shop the deal and unsettled points default to the acquirer (lore rule kan-leverage-ends-at-term-sheet). Learn the non-price deal-killer terms first (lore rule dixon-deal-killer-terms), and research how this acquirer has behaved between LOI and close before you sign anything (lore rule dixon-research-loi-conduct).

execution.rationale: The founder and counsel negotiate with the acquirer directly; leverage is spent in live conversation and cannot be delegated.

parts.title: Prepare the leak playbook now: the need-to-know list, the pre-agreed line with the acquirer, and what employees hear if it breaks

execution.rationale: The founder agrees the communication line with the acquirer and holds it; a leak response is credible only from the people in the deal.

links.when: the approach is real and the founder chooses to explore a sale

metadata.trigger: An acquirer reaches out: a corp-dev email, a partner-meeting invitation, or a direct offer to buy the company.
metadata.supportReason: Qualifying the approach, the board conversation, and the negotiation are founder work; an agent can assemble the data room, build the acquirer-conduct research file, and draft the need-to-know communication plan.

contextNeeded.query: the approach itself: who reached out, what they asked for, any deadline attached
whether the board knows, and any existing NDA or exclusivity with this party
